author: GamingBolt
description:
Dying Light: The Beast has been around for quite a few months now, and while the base game was already fantastic in its own right, Techland never really stopped bringing in major improvements to various aspects. 

Now, however, the studio has released a massive free update that brings in an entirely new way to re-experience the whole game, as well as a host of smaller-scale content that revolves around making traversal more interesting. 

Headlining the update is Restored Land, a new game mode, which essentially allows you to permanently kill all zombies in the entire game, with none of them respawning. This, of course, also means that resources are going to be more scarce, since those don't respawn either, and otherwise-repeatable activities can only be done once. 

Combined with harsher survival mechanics, like a flashlight that burns through batteries more quickly, this leads to a more intense playthrough that rewards thinking about situations before jumping in blindly.
title: Dying Light The Beast - Restored Land Is The Perfect Excuse To Revisit Castor Woods

author: GamingBolt
description:
Horror games are entering a bold new era. With more powerful hardware and increasingly ambitious developers, the genre is expanding far beyond simple jump scares into deeply psychological, cinematic, and mechanically inventive territory. 

From atmospheric slow burns and survival horror revivals to co-op chaos and narrative-driven nightmares, 2026 and beyond is stacked with plenty of games that are worth looking out for. To that end, we are taking a look at 20 new horror games that look ready to keep players sleeping with the lights on.
title: 20 NEW SCARY Horror Games of 2026 And Beyond

author: GamingBolt
description:
Crimson Desert is a massive game. And it’s packed according to its size and scope, which could lead to assumptions that it’s a rather empty title in its early hours. But for players who chose to engage with it in the way it's meant to be played, it has created the scope for adventures full of discovery and organic world building that have proven to be quite addictive. 

And yet, naysayers argue that its slow pacing points to a world that’s essentially devoid of fun things to do. Is that fair criticism or a lack of engagement with a game that does admittedly demand a ton of patience before it delivers a payoff? That’s what we’re here to discuss, as we take a look at why Crimson Desert might feel empty to some, but becomes chock full of fun to those who learn to love it the way it's meant to be.
title: Why Saying That Crimson Desert Has "Nothing Interesting" In Its First Dozen Hours Misses The Point
